claims.text: Adding a small amount of boron to phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys will improve glass-forming ability.
Adding a small amount of boron will enhance the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
The effective minor boron addition is on the order of 1–5 at.%.
The intervention should be effective when rapid quenching bypasses crystallization.
The intervention should benefit alloys having significant mixing enthalpy and atomic-size mismatch.
Excessive boron or an insufficient cooling rate may diminish the benefit.
Boron will increase local chemical heterogeneity.
Boron will improve atomic packing efficiency by enhancing negative mixing enthalpy.
The boron-induced structural changes will deepen the free-energy well of the amorphous state.
Minor boron additions will bond strongly with phosphorus and other constituent elements.
These interactions will impede the short-range atomic ordering that precedes crystallization.
Boron will increase atomic-size mismatch and enhance negative heats of mixing.
The resulting atomic configurations will hinder crystal nucleation.
Relative to the boron-free baseline, the boron-containing alloy will require a higher critical cooling rate to avoid crystallization.
Relative to the baseline, the boron-containing alloy will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature or delayed DSC exothermic peaks.
The improvement is confined to an approximately 1–5 at.% boron window.
Excessive boron could produce other phases.
Analogous mechanisms in which minor alloying additions improve phase stability are documented in high-entropy alloys.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts improved glass-forming ability, but the predicted outcome and falsification rule use a higher critical cooling rate as evidence of improvement. Requiring faster cooling to avoid crystallization ordinarily denotes poorer, rather than better, glass-forming ability, so the directional prediction is internally inconsistent with the stated outcome.
